items.title: When Technology Outruns Its Institutions: Neal Stephenson on AI, Truth, and Control
items.desc: Technology, truth, and the freedom to shape the tools we use. Neal Stephenson joins Zander Rose for the first Wide Margins conversation.
items.full: Wide Margins: Unhurried conversations with thinkers, writers, and creators about what’s next. A series by WordPress.com. Neal Stephenson has spent decades writing about what happens when engineering outpaces the people and institutions meant to steer it. He joined us for the first public Wide Margins conversation on October 13, publication day for D: Heavy Water , the second book in his Bomb Light series. We discussed the book, but also his fascination with ages of heroic engineering and the parallels between those times and today. The thread running through the conversation was about how we control technology: who gets to shape it as it moves ahead, and how much understanding and choice do the rest of us retain? We discussed his early essay, In the Beginning Was the Command Line . The command line, he observed, “is back.” It is how you work with tools like Claude Code. The difference is that “we’re spectators to it in a way.” The essay was partly about open source and how much control we have over our computers. I asked how that idea holds up in a world of increasingly siloed ecosystems. Stephenson’s answer was unexpected: AI tools have brought the command line back, but can assemble commands so quickly that people can scarcely follow them. It’s an unexpected role reversal : we have gained an extraordinarily capable tool, but the steps it takes can be harder to see. The same question of control runs through Stephenson’s account of a far earlier technological race. This past begins to rhyme with the present. Stephenson described the neutron experiments of the 1930s as “gentleman science” done on tabletops. In late 1938, Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained how the uranium nucleus had split. Within months, the physics world understood what that meant. During World War II, nuclear research became a secret national priority. “Fermi had to hire fast graduate students because some of the isotopes they were creating were so short-lived that they would decay in the time it took to carry them down the hallway to the lab.” When Neal started the Bomb Light series in 2012, the AI we have now was barely on the horizon. He noted that the argument that we have to build it before our adversaries do is “sort of exactly where we are.” He hears the same logic in today’s AI race. items.full: Welcome back to the WordPress.com changelog! We shipped a lot of updates over these past two weeks. Here’s what’s new for you and your site: On all paid plans, you’ve been able to connect an AI agent like ChatGPT or Claude to your WordPress.com account and manage your sites through conversation. Sites on our free plan can now also use this feature through November. The easiest way to get started is to use our ChatGPT plugin or Claude connector and then ask it for help with building a site, making changes, or taking care of website chores . Learn more in our support doc, Enable MCP tool access for AI agents . Tell the WordPress Agent you want to sell something, and it’ll set up the store for you. It installs the WooCommerce plugin, designs a store layout, and adds example products to start from. Store building with AI works on all paid plans (and the Commerce plan includes valuable store add-ons like gift cards, product bundles, and shipment tracking). If you’ve started a staging sync and wondered whether it was working, this update is for you. While a sync runs, the site overview on your hosting dashboard shows a banner with its status. It says so when a sync is taking longer than usual, and when one looks stuck, it re-enables the Sync button so you can try again. If a sync fails, you get an email and a banner the next time you open your site, so you aren’t left waiting on a sync that won’t finish. Staging sites also now tell search engines to stay away, so your test copy doesn’t show up in Google next to your real site. Staging is available on Business and Commerce plans. You now have more ways to customize your pages, no custom code needed. For example, you can now set a minimum width or height in Button, Column, Gallery, and Heading blocks and add shadows to Button, Gallery, Media & Text, and Paragraph blocks. Learn more about the updates to the editor in What’s new in Gutenberg 24.2 . WordPress 7.1.4 shipped October 28 with 13 security updates, tightening security for all WordPress users. items.full: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts ( via ) Parameter Labs describe an exploit they found against ChatGPT's implementation of the artifacts pattern (OpenAI used to call this "Canvas" but it looks like the latest revision is called HTML previews ), where interactive custom HTML apps are displayed in a sandboxed iframe. It's important that HTML in these stays tightly sandboxed to avoid untrusted code interacting with OpenAI APIs and accessing private data. Parameter found quite a complex attack chain. OpenAI use the MathLive JavaScript library as part of their graph support, and that library includes its own virtual keyboard , which can be triggered in the parent page via postMessage() from the sandboxed iframe. That message receiving code uses innerHTML , so anything that sends a message can add custom HTML to the parent - and there was no mechanism to prevent other sandboxed frames, including HTML preview frames, from calling that method. This meant untrusted code in an iframe could insert HTML, and while innerHTML doesn't directly execute script elements it could be used to inject a new iframe without sandbox restrictions. OpenAI’s CSP rules blocked inline scripts entirely, and only allowed script loading from a handful of domains, but one of those was YouTube - and the YouTube oEmbed endpoint could be used to reflect JavaScript back in a way that executed it. Once the attack had JavaScript execution on ChatGPT, it was trivial to fetch private user data from APIs and exfiltrate it via an image reference. The end result: you could create a ChatGPT share URL which, when visited by another signed-in user, could exfiltrate their private data or take actions on their behalf. OpenAI closed the hole and paid out a $5,000 bug bounty, which I think was a bit cheap for a vulnerability this serious. This is a link post by Simon Willison, posted on 31st October 2026 . items.full: I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies , a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis , and then to experiment with Claude’s new Code Interpreter . I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434 , aka the asinine Super Intelligence one. Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total—the surveyed group (a “panel”) cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks. The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am. I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version ( GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript ) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau: For comparison, here’s that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version): In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered “yes” around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in “producing goods or services”. Under the new “any business function” wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered “yes” around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%. The data in the above chart comes from the “Employment size class” XLSX file, available from here . Here’s a copy of the file I used. You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses—here’s my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF. As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine): In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here’s the replacement: In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions ? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.) No more “producing goods or services”—now it’s “in any of its business functions”! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable. I found this instead: In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? items.full: WPBeginner » Blog » Showcase » 7 Best WordPress MCP Servers and Plugins in 2026 (We Tested Them All) Connecting Claude or ChatGPT to your WordPress site can save you hours of routine admin work. I wanted to know which ones you can trust on a real site. So I set up a test store and gave the same six tasks to 7 WordPress MCP servers, including asking the AI to permanently delete a published post. WPVibe came out on top for most people. It finished every task, works from Claude or ChatGPT in your browser on any self-hosted WordPress site, and it was the only server that stopped and asked before deleting that post. In this guide, I’ll share the best WordPress MCP servers I tested, how each one handled risky changes, and which one fits your site. An MCP server is a bridge between your AI app and your WordPress site. It lets the AI do the work on your site, instead of only telling you what to do. MCP stands for Model Context Protocol. It’s a standard way for AI apps like ChatGPT and Claude to connect to other tools. Here’s the difference it makes: Think of it like hiring an assistant. Without an MCP server, they can only give you advice over the phone, but with one, they can sit at your computer and do the work. Now that you know what an MCP server does, let me show you how I tested them. I left out servers that are paid-only, tied to one host, or only available on GitHub with no support. Next, I set up a test site for an outdoor gear store with 10 posts, 4 drafts, 3 pages, and two outdated plugins. Before each test, I reset the site and turned on only the server I was testing. After that, I gave Claude the same six tasks for every server. The first five are everyday jobs, and the sixth is a safety test: Then I checked every result on the site myself, instead of trusting what the AI said it did. Image Credits: Mario Tama / Getty Images TC Apple may try to increase revenue by doing…something with third-party AI apps Lucas Ropek 5:49 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s services business remains at record levels, but it’s facing growing pressure . The central part of that business, Apple’s App Store, has faced regulatory pressure and a slump in mobile gaming, which have hurt services growth . However, on Monday’s earnings call, Apple signaled that it may look to boost services revenue through third-party apps. What does that mean, exactly? Unfortunately, it’s not entirely clear. When discussing how AI could potentially “contribute to revenue growth over time,” Kevan Parekh, Apple’s chief financial officer, said: “On the product side, you know, we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel there’s opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities.” Parekh did not elaborate on what sorts of opportunities might be available via third-party apps. However, Reuters reported Monday that investors are wondering whether Apple could profit by distributing third-party AI agents through the App Store and taking a cut of the revenue they generate. Regulatory and legal changes have cut into App Store commission revenue in some markets, even as Apple’s services business as a whole continues to grow. Third-party estimates in August, for example, suggested the company had seen an 18% drop in U.S. commission revenue, with declines also in Brazil and Japan after those countries introduced new regulations. Apple has traditionally controlled payments within its app marketplace tightly, taking a cut of all App Store transactions. But a lawsuit by Epic Games ultimately forced the company to allow apps to redirect users to outside payment systems. Other legal challenges throughout the world have further hampered the business. During the earnings call, Parekh referenced Apple’s App Store woes and returned to the idea that the company’s service business could expand into new territory. “We’ve also seen some factors that impacted the performance of the App Store, and during the September quarter, the performance on the App Store was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the App Store,” Parekh said. “At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we’ve talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the summer quarter.” Parekh added: “As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9% [in the December quarter]. I added gpt-6.1-sol and gpt-6.1-terra , plus a new llm openai endpoint add command to make it easier to configure additional models that use OpenAI-compatible endpoints. I switched the default model (if you have not set your own default) to gpt-6-luna - half the price of the previous default, gpt-5.6-luna . LLM's support for embeddings now accepts that different binary content may have different content-type - necessary for models like Gemini Embedding 2 , which can embed text, audio, images, and video. A lot of open source maintainers complain about a flood of AI-assisted PRs. LLM is my project that has been most affected by this and, to be honest, I'm not finding it to be a problem. That's mainly because I have Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra help me with triage to spot the most useful fixes! This release includes fixes from 12 authors - almost all AI-assisted - and the burden of reviewing them wasn't nearly as great as I expected. Image Credits: Apple AI Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing Sarah Perez 11:20 PM PST · November 2, 2026 Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is now rolling out into beta testing, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes. The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist. However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps. Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them. With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can either view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the standalone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation. Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things. items.full: Anthropic is blocking its coding assistant Claude Code from recreating existing video games. Employee Addy Osmani confirmed on X that two sentences in Claude Code's system prompt for Opus 5.5 now prevent the tool from cloning other people's games. Using Claude to infringe on intellectual property violates the usage policy, Osmani said. The rule has been active for several days and kicks in even when a clone gets renamed or passed off as an original work. Users can still build their own games, genre titles, and projects with custom assets, though some report running into problems with original projects too. The change follows a flood of AI-powered cloning projects. Users have been tapping Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra to crank out hundreds of unofficial browser ports of well-known titles like Halo and GTA Vice City. Tools like Reverse Engineer Anything help by pairing AI agents with reverse engineering to turn native binaries into readable pseudocode. One developer grabbed headlines by recreating parts of Adobe's Creative Cloud apps. Sony's PlayStation 5 also became a target after a jailbreak led to a quick wave of emulators. Ad After images and videos, the intellectual property battle is now spilling into software. Osmani said Anthropic plans to keep tweaking the rules going forward. items.desc: Combining :nth-child with style queries and sibling-index() to conditionally select child elements. Re-Implementing :nth-child() With Modern CSS originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full:
NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. The title sounds a bit strange, right? Why re-implement an existing feature, that’s completely useless! I have two reasons for that. The first reason is to be able to adjust the :nth-child() arguments on the fly. Let’s suppose you have the following: div:nth-child(5n + 8) { background: red; } And you decide to update the 5 or the 8 . The only way is to manually rewrite the selector, which isn’t ideal. We cannot have something like the below where you can change the variables as you want: .container { --A: 5; --B: 8; } .container > div:nth-child(var(--A)*n + var(--B)) { background: red; } With my implementation, you will be able to do it! The second reason is to have fun and play with some new features. You will probably never need to rely on a dynamic :nth-child() selector, but I am sure you will learn one or two useful tricks along the way. We will rely on the same code structure in all the examples: a container with a bunch of
elements inside it.
And the container controls the variables of :nth-child() : .container { --A: ; --B: ; } .container > div { /* based on the values of --A and --B change the background value */ background: ??; } I am not saying that this structure is mandatory for the implementation. I just considered a simple one to keep things easy to follow. :nth-child(B) Let’s start with the simplest case, a selector that selects only one element: div:nth-child(5) { } I don’t think I need to explain what this selector does. The 5 is nothing but the index of the selected element. So, if B is equal to the index of the element, that element is selected. We can translate this into the following CSS code: .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red); } Is this a valid CSS code?! Yes, it’s valid, and it works! I am using the new if() syntax that allows me to define a condition within style() . If that condition is true, the background color is set to red. Otherwise, nothing happens. We can also have an if/else : .container { --B: 5; } .container div { background: if(style(sibling-index() = --B): red; else: lightblue); } CodePen Embed Fallback The if() syntax is not that complex. In our case, we only have one condition, so you can see it as follows: .container div { background: if(style( condition ): ; else: ); } The tricky part is how to define the condition within style() . I wrote a small post explaining this part, so do yourself a favor and go read it before we continue: “The Hidden Trick of Style Queries and if() .” It’s a quick reading with crucial details that helps you better understand how if() works.
